title: HOLY CRAP
body1:
Reclamation is not only a physical act but also a conceptual one. This work is a statement of reclaiming peace and solitude without the subservience to any higher power, whether it be a God or a city council. Instead of a holy torture in the apse, this chapel is orientated toward a crucified martyr of Antepavilion: a shark. Inspired by medieval construction methods, this structure is frozen in its scaffolding stage. The scaffolding itself is the ornamentation.

Benches of reclaimed red louro and brick line the edge of the barge's hull so people can recant their woes in peace. The exterior appears somewhat chaotic due to the crisscrossing structural ties and supports but the interior is more understated. Those arriving with frustration and anger can decompress in the Chapel of Scrap.
body2: This project turns the material usage on its head. The Red Louro, once finishing material, becomes a structural element by binding layers of the strips together to reinforce each other. The tetrapak sheets, typically a cheap solution for cladding auxiliary structures, is used as the interior finish of this skeletal cathedral. The reclaimed brick is used to anchor the structure for stability: red brick for the columns, blue brick for the seating elements.

title: CROSSING OVER
h2: the path of spirits glow in light, crossing over, into night
body1:
Where do we go when we die? It's a question that eats at anyone who has lost a loved one. This installation seeks to offer some peace, or maybe a challenge, to that question. A series of glowing paths slowly make their way back and forth across the canal, like spirits briefly passing overhead on their way to a new home.

Visitors who approach this installation will find it takes on different forms from different angles. The sheer fabric sails bunch in places, adding layers of opacity or transparency depending on the viewer's position. Due to the varying angles of the sails, their different lengths and the multiple points of intersection, an observer will find the piece comes alive in different ways each time they visit.
body2:
The paths of light move at different paces — at times catching up to one another, like several beings finding each other and converging after wandering alone, or parting as they pass. Beyond the calming effect of the lighting, the hope is that this work becomes a place of reflection for someone to contemplate love and loss.

The ethereal effect is achieved with a linear programmable LED strip, moving several segments of light along the path in synchronicity to suggest an abstract figure passing through the fabric, its silhouette blurred by the sheer diffusion. The installation is composed of three sails of weatherproof sheer fabric, each sandwiching a linear LED strip at its vertical midpoint, tensioned across the canal with lightweight cables that hold the piece — and its shape against the wind.

title: MIRROR – MIRROR
h2: a station to connect communities and individuals
body1:
The time we spend waiting for things in public is, more often than not, wasted time. We might treat these rare moments of boredom with apathy, or worse—disdain. We wait with other humans surrounding us, but we turn inwards, to our phones, our thoughts, our worries.

If the places we spent time waiting around provided more opportunity to look out of ourselves, maybe we could reconnect with our community or our fellow humans.
body2:
This bus rapid transit station is located in a prominent commercial corridor which connects unique neighborhoods, old and new. The residents are as unique as the neighborhoods they live in. This station gives the residents, who will soon rely on this transit line, a chance to connect with each other using a simple tool—the mirror.

The quote embedded in the polished steel panel comes from Italo Calvino's Invisible Cities. Its purpose is to draw the attention of the riders to the surface overhead. In reading the quote, provided in English and Spanish, the riders might catch a glance of their fellow rider as they too read the quote above.

Soft lighting and penetrations in the structure provide safety and visibility of users. The composite concrete surfaces are easily cleanable and the reinforced traffic barrier protects those on the platform from oncoming traffic.

title: THE HOT SEAT
body1: Every year the Pittsburgh Polar Bear Club jumps into the frigid waters of the Monongahela River. It's been described as quick and exhilarating, something "The Hot Seat" was inspired by. Sponsored by Epic Metals, this design marries the precise, thin, and reflective nature of metal decking with the stark, raw quality of steel members to create a structure that celebrates the vibrancy of metal.
body2:
The interior changing rooms contrast the cold exterior with the warmth of cork lined floors, canvas partitions, and seats heated by coals which sit in a bed made from metal decking. The entire structure is designed for extremely fast assembly and disassembly, using self-locking hinge joints.

Within the structure you can experience a blend of elements that are not only useful but comfortable as well. The exterior caters to swimmer and spectator alike, providing seating which is heated by the thermal bridge from the interior and also faces south, towards the sun. Finally, you can enjoy a hot beverage at the built-in bar and continue on your way.

title: PLASTIC PAVILION
h2: Can a community be brought together by their trash?
body1:
Every day, trash bins are filled with plastic cups embossed with recycling symbols. But if you follow the journey of that cup, does it actually get recycled? Most often, the answer is no. It lives its many hundreds of years of life sitting in a landfill or polluting our water.

So, we were curious—could we take hundreds of discarded plastic cups and turn them into a shelter? A core goal of this experiment was to create a replicable process with somewhat of a recipe book for anyone to experiment with, as well.
body2:
Despite the utilitarian design, the repurposed material that came out of the process also proved to have an inherent beauty. We wanted to show the public that regardless of their local authorities' indifference toward recycling, they have the power to change their impact from negative to positive.

We wanted to take off the shelf tools—a paper shredder, a heat press, silicone baking sheets, zipties, and a few hundred plastic cups—and make something with longevity from all these disposable products. If we could create this pavilion over a couple months, imagine what an entire community could do with their collective trash and their imagination.

In collaboration with Cy Kim.

title: A (DYS)FUNCTIONAL FUTURE
h2: a pavilion for one day's dreams
body1:
“Give me your tired, your poor, your huddled masses yearning to breathe free.” Emma Lazarus's words are etched into the base of the Statue of Liberty — a promise of opportunity for anyone willing to reach for it. So many people dream of starting something of their own, of sharing what they make, yet never get the chance. Not from a lack of will, but a lack of resources, motivation, or access to a public space of their own.

What if those dreamers could, for one day, see it realized? This proposal is a swiss army knife of functions with no branding and no history, but real presence within Hong Kong's deTour 2025. The space can be booked by one person for one day — an online lottery grants temporary ownership of a small plot of public space that is otherwise entirely out of reach.
body2:
Purposefully dysfunctional in plan, the pavilion resists conventional use. It isn't a turnkey workspace — it demands adaptation. Three openings with pivoting panels serve entry, a service counter, and a communal table, formed by three intersecting gabled façades: too small for a large operation, but enough, for the determined, to be the spark that ignites their future.

The structure is built from Polygood Translucent Pink recycled plastic panels — visually rich, easy to cut, drill, and mount. Over time it will evolve, layered by each person's use of it, becoming a dynamic centerpiece for public interaction.

title: BORROWED TIME
body1:
Our society runs on a symbiotic relationship of lent and borrowed time. This installation explores how we lend our time to others, or spend the time others lend us. Visitors lie back on a large platform beneath a conical canopy, watching a gently expanding light projection above them — but the display only activates when another visitor steps onto a small pressure pad off to the side. Step off, and the projection fades.

From the pad, the time lender can't see the light show they've made possible — but they've given someone else a moment they wouldn't otherwise have had. The piece is built for all ages, but speaks most directly to teens and young adults: a physical lesson in empathy, inequity, and the quiet joy of giving up something for someone else.
body2: The installation has four parts: a rubber pressure pad wired to a projector power supply, two fabric canopies tensioned with PVC rings and lightweight cable — one over the pad, one as a screen for the light — and a lounging platform built from truncated MDF sections around a simple fiberboard projector housing, the whole surface finished in durable acrylic felt.

title: F--K
body1:
The difference between a stranger and a friend is a conversation. The places we feel most comfortable talking to strangers are often intimate, shared spaces — a fire, if there's a real atmosphere of intimacy around it. At a festival, though, most people arrive as strangers and stay inside the groups they came with; gathered around one single fire, the space quickly feels closed off. The Space Between decentralizes that focal point, scattering smaller, more intimate spaces where people can organically encounter one another.

It's a bridge between strangers, a spatial experience unfolding between two structures, and a use that isn't strictly dictated. To break the social barrier of talking to someone new, at least one person has to let their guard down — and the most effective way to do that is through play. The Space Between is formed by two giant letters, an ‘f’ and a ‘k,’ for fritz-kola, offering places to sit, climb, lie down, or dance.
body2:
The letters do double duty: they tie the structure directly to the brand rather than applying it after the fact, and their forms create narrow, raised pathways that give the grass room to breathe while forcing people to pass close to one another — close enough for an ‘excuse me’ that can start a conversation. The ‘f’ bends away from an existing tree and wraps around an added fire pit; the ‘k’ weaves between the remaining trees so the structure feels embedded in the park rather than imposed on it.

Built from recycled and easily repurposed materials: reclaimed wood planks and beams form the raised platform, painted metal tubing frames the canopy and walls for later reuse as scaffolding, and canvas or recycled plastic tarps enclose it — letting firelight show through while keeping out wind and rain.

title: HALLOWED GROUND
h2: a war fought with paperwork, honored in the physical world
body1:
If a war is fought with paperwork, how can it be honored in the physical world? This project dramatizes a legal battle with Hackney Council as a symbolic narrative: a thriving community space, assaulted by bureaucratic power, reborn as a memorial to its own past and its people.

From a distance it reads as cold armor — corrugated metal cladding, easily mistaken for another stair bulkhead. Closer in, the structure turns whimsical: a corner floats above a hint of water, a stark black plane slices through the façade, and the gray cladding reveals itself as a mosaic of recycled tetrapak. A deliberately narrow path forces visitors to the canal's edge, face to face with the sharks, before the space opens overhead into a highly textured black interior — charred-looking OSB walls, a shallow pool of black water and rock, and a narrow walkway of unpainted Red Louro lath, the only light surface in the room.
body2:
A basin of salt sits by the entrance. Visitors are invited to take a handful and toss it across the water, watching it swirl and dissolve — a small ritual to cleanse the site of its bad spirits, or its bureaucrats, and pay respect to what guards the entrance. It's optional; the space rewards quiet contemplation just as well, watching sunlight patterns move across the black pool.

The project is built to be taken apart. Bolted, modular panels in standard sheet sizes mean less waste at disassembly and near-perfect stock for whatever comes next. Tetrapak-clad walls on a wood frame, painted OSB interiors, a simple waterproofed timber pool, and a walking surface of Red Louro lath and painted framing — a structure with a life, an afterlife, and maybe, with Antepavilion 2026, a reincarnation.

title: SYMBIOTICA
h2: a ceremony of trees, flowers, and birds
body1:
Symbiotica unfolds in three movements. A ten-minute preamble introduces the performance and primes participants for mindful participation. In the twenty-minute ceremony that follows, three deities appear at their altars and pull people from the crowd into their respective tribes — the trees, the flowers, and the birds — each given a symbolic cloak and mask that offers the anonymity, and the sameness, to let go.

A fifteen-minute performance of guided, improvised movement follows, led by each deity: the flowers move with elegance, graceful waves, gentle spinning and humming; the birds with freedom, fast and piercing through the crowd, flailing and squawking; the trees with strength, rigid, stomping, marching, shushing like wind through branches.
body2: The final movement is a seventy-five-minute celebration where all three tribes come together — glowing cubes raised above the crowd like a giant chandelier as the groups blend into one.
